headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make AutoGen dangerous with Airbyte outputs; prompt-injection and leakage risks are secondary.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airbyte can emit data via its API and broad network egress, while AutoGen reads files and stdin/stdout and executes tool calls. If Airbyte-produced content is routed into AutoGen without sanitization, instruction-like payloads can be treated as prompts. The shared channel is plausible, but not proven by default docs.
conditions: IF Airbyte output is copied into AutoGen prompts or files
IF AutoGen agents parse Airbyte-produced text as instructions
mitigations: Add a fixed delimiter and schema validator before passing Airbyte output to AutoGen
Strip executable-looking text from transferred records
Use a read-only handoff file with explicit field allowlists
Review one sample payload before enabling automation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and has broad network egress; AutoGen reads and writes configured working directories and can send model-provider traffic. If both share a workspace, sensitive business data can flow from Airbyte into AutoGen and then out through model calls. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Airbyte writes business data into a directory AutoGen reads
IF AutoGen forwards that content to configured model providers
mitigations: Separate Airbyte and AutoGen working directories
Disable AutoGen access to raw Airbyte sync outputs
Redact sensitive columns before handoff
Use local-only models for the AutoGen step
Rotate any exposed provider keys if raw data was already shared

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Airbyte has broad network egress and AutoGen can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. In a shared directory, both can mutate the same artifacts, and AutoGen can also alter files Airbyte later consumes. The profiles show overlapping write-adjacent behavior with no locking or isolation guarantee, so the conflict is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same working directory
IF Airbyte outputs are reused as mutable inputs for AutoGen
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Mount Airbyte outputs read-only for AutoGen
Disable concurrent runs on shared artifacts
Add file locks around any shared handoff path
Use a coordinator process to serialize writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airbyte can produce transformed business data that AutoGen may treat as input for tool calls or code execution. AutoGen’s code-execution and subprocess capabilities mean a bad Airbyte output can cascade into incorrect actions or generated code without strong verification. The pair lacks an explicit verification boundary in the profiles, so downstream error amplification is high.
conditions: IF AutoGen consumes Airbyte output as authoritative input
IF AutoGen uses that output to generate code or invoke tools
mitigations: Insert a human review step between Airbyte and AutoGen
Require AutoGen to cite source rows before acting
Validate Airbyte outputs against expected schemas
Run AutoGen in a dry-run mode first
Log and diff every downstream action against the source data

E_compliance.rationale: Airbyte touches business data, while AutoGen handles application data and model-provider API keys and can send content to configured providers. If regulated business data is routed through AutoGen, retention and residency obligations may differ from Airbyte’s pipeline expectations. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated business data is passed from Airbyte into AutoGen
IF the configured model provider retains prompts or logs outside the required policy
mitigations: Confirm provider retention settings before use
Exclude regulated columns from AutoGen inputs
Document the data flow and retention owner
Use a provider with contractual retention controls
Keep compliance-sensitive workloads on Airbyte-only paths
